author: Abby Foster
title: What Apple Inc. (NASDA:AAPL)’s new HomePod will bring to us on Feb, 9
text:
January 28, 2018 What Apple Inc. (NASDA:AAPL)’s new HomePod will bring to us on Feb, 9 
Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) is projected to ship the HomePod on February 9, with outstanding sale number attributed to the considerable effort company has put into audio processing for the device. Matt Hines, audio expert and product manager of Spire by iZotope has explained some of the technical problems that Apple along with other smart speaker manufacturers have to overcome to offer a high-quality audio experience in a comprehensive variety of environments. 
The initial problem the company and similar firms confront while creating an intelligent speaker, like the HomePod, is to make sure an optimal audio experience for the user, irrespective of where they are in the room. Hines, guest on this week’s AppleInsider Podcast, said that the actual position of the user can radically affect the sound from a normal speaker, with the issue multifaceted by local acoustics. 
Hines suggested that when a speaker is moved around room it alters the sound reflections dramatically, for instance a loss of bass frequencies while moving towards the corner of a room. The reflections can burgeon the sound in diverse ways while bouncing around the room, probably leading some resonant frequencies to become incoherently louder. It is an effect that is specifically noticeable for lengthier wavelengths. He advises that users might hear abrupt, intense variations in frequency levels depending on where the ear is, that is why bass might vanish in the corner of a room. 
Items positioned within the local environment can also alter sound quality, with soft furnishings engrossing some noise while stiffer surfaces have an inclination to reflect it. That is why places pertaining to audio consumption or audio production, like a high-end home cinema room or a recording studio, carefully choose the materials they put on their floors, walls and ceilings to manage the sound up to the user’s requirements. 
The company is using six microphones and a digital signal processor (DSP) to know the environment based on its acoustics, and adjust the device’s output to coordinate with its physical location and the room’s audio profile. The DSP along with this adaptive acoustic processing system would also assist when the HomePod will get its stereo audio feature through a future update, one that will provide stereo audio split between two HomePods. 
The beamforming technology enables the HomePod to decide the position of the user corresponding to the device, and then adjust its microphone settings to better attain audio from that direction. About Abby Foster
